title: The 3 Reasons Smart Leaders Produce Weak Strategies
author: Marc
summary: Drawing on more than twenty years advising executive teams on strategy, the author identifies three reasons smart leaders still produce weak strategic plans: nobody ever actually taught them to build a strategy rather than just learn about one, frameworks like SWOT or Porter's Five Forces get filled in as a substitute for genuinely hard thinking, and finished plans avoid real trade-offs by setting goals for every department so nobody feels left out. He traces all three back to a single root cause he calls the 'Template Trap' — recycling last year's deck, updating the numbers and buzzwords, and calling the result a strategy without ever diagnosing the market or committing to what the company will not do. He offers a one-line diagnostic test: if a competitor could paste their logo on your strategy document and change almost nothing, it isn't a strategy at all.
points: Even an MBA teaches executives ABOUT strategy without ever having them build one, leaving most leaders to rely on a two-day workshop and a SWOT template from years ago.
Frameworks like SWOT and Porter substitute the feeling of progress (a filled-in canvas) for the hard choices a real strategy requires, since no framework makes the trade-offs for you.
A plan that sets goals for every department at once ('growth,' 'efficiency,' and 'innovation' all together) is really a document that commits the company to nothing.
The 'Template Trap' — recycling last year's deck, refreshing the market slide, and filling every box — produces a document that leadership approves but that changes nothing six months later.
His diagnostic test for a real strategy: could a competitor paste their logo on your strategy deck and change almost nothing? If yes, it's a template, not a strategy.
quotes: Even an MBA teaches you ABOUT strategy. It never has you build one.

SWOT, Porter, Blue Ocean: everyone applies the same tools to the same market. Filling in a canvas feels like progress, but no framework makes the hard choices for you. So the framework produces a document, and the real questions stay open.

Goals for every department, so nobody feels left out. “Growth,” “efficiency” and “innovation” all at once, with no choice between them. Nothing the company decided NOT to do. A plan everyone approves because it commits nobody.

You take last year’s document, or a template from your previous company. You update the numbers, refresh the market slide, add the current buzzwords. You fill every box: mission, SWOT, pillars, initiatives, KPIs. The deck looks complete, so leadership approves it. Six months later, nothing has changed in how the company operates.
Here’s a quick test. Take your current strategy document and ask: “Could a competitor paste their logo on this deck and change almost nothing?” If yes, you have a template, not a strategy.
